title: Neutralize the negative
header_line: Jose's analysis of a book we are still naming. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: Can you stay calm when you are blamed?
A student said that staying calm shows your strength as a leader because you are not shaken, and it is a pattern interrupt because they expect you to be defensive.
Another said that the chapter ahead is about neutralizing the negative and reinforcing the positive.
A student described the shape of a good reply: first the emotion, then the transition into control, then layering more evidence.
Jose said you combine the two with a repertoire of transitions: even though you are angry, you give me a surprising sense of confidence. Now I am leading.

groups.heading: Do not defend, do not blame

lines.text: Jose said that when someone attacks, we tend to defend and throw back, and that is a lack of discipline. In relationships we blame before we even understand where the other person is coming from.
He said that it is very difficult to say I disagree, and showed the group a way to avoid saying it.
He said that great leaders expect surprises, and cannot let the surprises throw them off their game.

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write the last time you were blamed.
Write the calm reply you will use.
Write the transition that moves from emotion to control.
Write the evidence you would add.

check.q: What did a student say staying calm is?
What did Jose say defending and blaming show?
What did Jose say great leaders expect?

recap: Do not defend or blame. Interrupt the pattern. Lead.
